blocks.x: Thank you, and good evening. Tonight, we're particularly fortunate. We saved this as our first broadcast of the new year because the man we're about to introduce is without a doubt one of the most famous characters who has ever come from the city of New Orleans. I speak of none other than Nick LaRocca, who is the organizer, the leader, the trumpet man with the original Dixieland jazz band, and Nick, I don't think, has ever had too much of a chance to tell his message, and we thought that tonight we would celebrate an entire new deal in the jazz world by talking to and with Nick LaRocca. Now, we might explain first that Nick is 71 years old and while he's still in good health, is not able to get around the way he did just a few years ago, and we have asked his consent to interview him by means of telephone, which will explain the beep sounds you'll hear occasionally. Now, he is standing by, so we want to take you at this time to the private home of Mr. Nick LaRocca. Nick, are you there? I am here, Dave. I'm certainly glad to have this chance to talk with you, and I'd like to have you tell us as much about yourself as you can. First of all, I was right when I said that you were 71 years young.
Well, that is correct.
How do you feel?
Well, I feel all right, but only my legs, that's all. They don't get me around.
That's right. That's why you couldn't come down to the studios to talk with us.
That is correct.

And now, we want you to tell us as much as you can about the original Dixieland band and the old-time music that was in fashion. Now, first of all, Nick, when did you start to play music in New Orleans?
Well, I started picking up a horn in 1898. It was around the Spanish-American wall.
I was about nine years old then.
Uh-huh.
And I tried to teach myself. My father happened to be a musician, and I'd take his cornet and sneak it down the back in an empty house in the next block, and I'd try to learn on it.
You mean to tell me he didn't want you to play music?
No, he didn't want me to play music.

Well, it's a good thing you had a head of your own, otherwise the world would have never known anything about Dixieland music. That's right. Now, let me ask you this. About how old were you when you first started to play professionally?
Professionally? I was around maybe 16 or 17. I was around 1908.
Uh-huh.
I had played in other little string bands before that, 1902, 1903, with small outfits that we'd go serenading around the Irish Channel.
Yeah.
There were string outfits.
Uh-huh.
And I had the only brass instrument in the band.
Now, you, of course, played the old-fashioned cornet. You did not play trumpet as they do today.

No, they didn't have a trumpet. In fact, I had a high-pitched instrument, and they used to break all the strings, so I had to have a piece of pipe made by a tin smith to lure the instrument so they wouldn't have to pull these strings so tight.

Well, that's a wonderful story. In case our friends don't realize it, he is speaking of the pitch of musical instruments today, which is standardized at 440, which is A, and in the old days they used 445 vibrations per second. That's all changed. Nick, now, you at this time did not have a band of your own. Is this correct? You used to play with other people.
No, no, I'd play with any bunch that wanted me. It was free music with serenades and different places, like we'd go to different parties and play for nothing.
Yeah.
And we were known as no beer, no music bunch.

Now, Nick, I think at this time we'll give them a fair sample of the kind of music that came from you when you were a very young man, so let them hear first. The Dixieland Jazz Band, which is actually the name of the song, it's the Dixieland Jazz Band, spelled J-A-S-S, which was the original spelling of jazz. Now, this recording was made many years ago and has been reissued, and the result is that it's not quite up to what we would like to call broadcast standard today, but it's still wonderful music. Let's hear it now. The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, The Dixieland Jazz Band, ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ And that was the original Dixieland jazz band playing a tune called the Dixieland Jazz Band. Now, we still have on the phone our old friend Nick LaRocka, the daddy, the granddaddy, the great-grandfather, calling what you want, of jazz. Now, Nick, let me talk to you. We had gotten up to about 1908, and by then you were just about to become a professional musician. Is that right?
That's right.
Did you have a band of your own yet?
I did have a band. It was called the Rockus Band.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
But I had played so much free music that people hired me and used to come get me for nothing, didn't want to pay me, so I started taking jobs with other bands.
Uh-huh. What other bands did you play with?
Well, I played with Joe Baraka, Leon Rapolo, and Bill Gallaty.
Uh-huh.
Susu Ramis, Harry Nunes, many bands. Then, around 1912, I was asked to play with Jack Lane.
Uh-huh. Oh, and this is the famous Papa Lane you used to call him.
That's right, old man Lane. He played ragtime drums, and he asked me if I'd take a job in his band.
Yeah.
And I'd take the job in his band, and I became the leader of that band up from around 1912 to 1916.
Now, let's go back just a minute, Nick. You say this was Papa Lane's ragtime band. That's right. Well, weren't we playing jazz in New Orleans back from 1908 on?
No, sir, we were playing ragtime. That record you played was made in 1917.

I see. Now, in other words, all the New Orleans bands, whether they were colored or white, were at the time playing ragtime music. That's right. That is what we call ragtime today. Did they call it ragtime then, too?
Yes, it was called ragtime. Uh-huh. It had the syncopation to a four-beat music, but ours was syncopated to a march beat, or a two-beat.

Uh-huh. In other words, we still call it two-beat music today, by the way. That is right. And so there was no jazz in New Orleans or anywhere else at the time we speak of, which was up to roughly 1912 and 1913. Is this correct?
Even up to 1916.
All right. Now, about when did you organize your first band?

Well, I was playing on a court here on Canal Street, and Harry James is an impresario. He heard me play, and he asked me if I could furnish him a band. So at this time, I used to play at the Old Haymarket, and they had several men playing that I knew, and we formed that band and brought that band to Chicago. And that was in March of 1916.
March of 1916.
That's right.

In other words, as everybody believes falsely, you did not go directly to New York from New Orleans. No. First went to Chicago. And let me go back for just one minute, Nick. You mentioned the name Harry James. Now, this is a new generation of people, and everybody thinks Harry James is a trumpet player. The Harry James Mr. LaRocca is speaking of was a nightclub or a cabaret manager, as they used to call him in those days. And it was just a similarity in names. I knew Harry James, too, very well. In fact, we all did. He had gotten to be quite a person around New Orleans. But to get back to this now, how long did you fellas stay in Chicago?

Nine months. We were there nine months. It was in Chicago that I assumed we were going to be a flop, and I said to the boys, let me swing one of those things that we played in the carnival parades and put some syncopation to it. I see they're doing a one step here. I used to dance very well.
Mm-hmm.
Very good dancer.
Uh-huh.
And we tried one, and the people hollered, and they hollered, give us more jazz. In less than a week, they had the police and firemen to come out there.
Now, tell me this, Nick. In other words, when you first went to Chicago, then the band wasn't playing jazz there either.
No, no. We hadn't changed the rhythm there.
In other words, the band went up there more...
We developed it there by watching these people who were trying to imitate Vine and Castle doing the castle walk, which was a one step.
I see. So in other words, you didn't even leave New Orleans as a jazz band. You went up there as actually a dance band.
The word I never heard before in my life until I ate Chicago.
And that's when the word jazz was born.
That's right. And Harry James picked that up, and he added it to the name.
Uh-huh.
And he called us the original Dixieland jazz band because after our success there, brought many boys from New Orleans. And every band was calling himself a New Orleans jazz band.
Right. Now, speaking of jazz bands, Nick, let me interrupt you. Didn't you write a tune called At the Jazz Band Ball? That's right. Well, we...
Between Shields and myself.

That's right. That's Larry Shields, who, of course... Harry Shields, rather. The clarinet player. And we have a recording of it now by the original Dixieland jazz band at the jazz band ball. 楽 The End The End The End The End Fine. And that was at the jazz band Ball. Now to get back to our interview with world famous Nick LaRocca, the daddy of jazz. Nick, for the next record we have selected, which will be coming up in a moment or two, we have Delivery Stable Blues. Now, that's a very interesting name. Was there a story connected with this at all?

Well, there was a story connected with it. There was a litigation. One of the men in the early Chicago bands that I had let go, he wanted a piece of it, which I thought he wasn't entitled to, because the tunes were mine.
Uh-huh.
And he had some publisher to go on to work and put it out, and I had taken an injunction and stopped him.

Mm-hmm. Now, may I ask you this? Uh, you were able to prove, of course, in court that you had composed the Liver Stable Blues, because I noticed that the copyright is in your name. That's right. Now, let me ask you this. In your composition, how did you manage to write the music? Because...
Well, I'll tell you, being a faker and not being able to line new tunes as fast as the people would...

I had to have something new tunes. So I'd take some of these old tunes like Shine on Harvest Moon. Take the chord construction. I made the jazz band ball out of it. I'd take old pieces like the Georgia Camp Meeting Ball. I made the fidgeted feet out of it. The last part I put on myself. But the rest of it are the same chord constructions. But you know, I played a little chords on the piano. And I understood it. Most old fakers you will find can play three or four instruments.

Yes, that we know. Now, Nick, let me clarify this. Because remember, you and I are talking as musicians. But the people who are listening to us don't know exactly what we mean. Out of the whole original jazz band that you had in Chicago and later in New York, the only one who could actually read music was the piano player, Russell Robinson.
Well, that came in later years after Ragus had died.
Yeah.
And we couldn't get a piano player. And Robinson had learned these tunes off the phonograph record. And he came to New York. And we had tried out so many piano players.
Mm-hmm.
We had Eddie Shields come up from New Orleans. And he couldn't fit in. We sent him back.
Well, in other words, originally none of the men could read music.
No, none of us read music. We were fakers.
Uh-huh.
And we understood one another. It was just like, I don't know, like you had a cogwheel. I was always one known to hit him. Then the way I was going.

That's a wonderful thing. Now, so in other words, you revised each of these tunes. And it was known among you fellas by a completely different name. Is that correct? That's correct. And that's a very interesting point. That's a story I've never heard before. That fidgety feet then was originally, you say.
It came. No, it wasn't originally. I get me wrong. I won't get no royalties on it.
No, I know what you mean.
I said I took the chord construction.
Yeah.
And on top of that, I'll...
You put your own...
Melody.
Well, you can't copyright a C chord. You know that, don't you? No, that's right. But I'm telling you, the melody's entirely different.
And that's where it came from.
Yes.
If anybody wants to look it up, all they got to do is compare them. And they'll see that I have told the truth.
Well, I can see that. Now, let's go on with your story, Nick. You fellas did not come back to New Orleans after you were in Chicago.
No, we went on to New York in Rising River, where we're the greatest sensation that ever hit Broadway in 50 years. We turned Broadway upside down.
Well, that's what we know. That's where you actually made history. That's right. Was in New York. Now, which year was that again?
Rising River's Cafe at 58 in Columbus Circle.
Just an interesting side note. I'm looking at one of your old pictures here, and I noticed that you played cornet originally left-handed.
That is right. I'm a left-hand cornet player.
I just happened to catch that for a moment. I thought the picture had been developed backwards, but I see that it is the truth.
I was left-handed, and I didn't have a left-handed instrument. I played on a right-handed instrument, but I was left-handed.
Uh-huh.

Well, there's a little more story to that, Dave. Well, why don't you tell it to us? Well, in 1918, when the draft came on, Edwards was put into the Army. I came to New Orleans, and I picked up another great man and a good musician, Emil Christ.
We had Emil on the air with us a couple of weeks back, and he spoke very well to you, so tell us about that.

Well, Emil, after we rehearsed in a few weeks, we went back and fulfilled our contract. We woke up until January, in the middle of January, where we went to London, England, and introduced jazz into England.
Well, I have a copy of that record, too, of one of the tunes which was composed while you were in England. That's the satanic blues, it's called.
That's right, Emil and Fields.

That's right, they're credited with authorship. Now, will you tell me this, Nick, is there any story behind the satanic blues? In other words, these fellas didn't read too much music either. Did they take this, or did they just act a composer?

They'll give me an idea of how, why don't you make a tune on this? Well, it was a cooperative band, and it didn't make no difference whose name went on the tunes. So I played the melody, and like I say, Shields put the lace on it, and the trombone players sewed it up, whether he was Edwards or Christian, they sewed it up, and that was the way I started playing.
Well, before we play this record, let me just ask you one thing, Nick. There's been a lot of misunderstanding. The original Dixieland jazz band was composed of good friends. Isn't this so?
That's right.
We were all good friends. That's right.

We had no enemies. It was a cooperative band, and the money was split equally. I did all the business for the band. I did the leading on getting the jobs, and everything else was my job. And when it came to splitting the money up, it was a five-way split. There's some of the boys still living. They'll tell you they got what's coming to them.

Yes, well, that's what a lot of people don't realize, that these men are still around. It's not quite as long ago as we'd like to think. So many people think that the original Dixieland jazz band was something that was around just before the Revolutionary War.
Well, that was caused by a lot of modern-day writers.

Yes, I know. And that's why we're so anxious to get all of your messages we can, Nick LaRocca. But at this time, let's let our audience hear the tune that you fellas composed while you were in England called The Satanic Blues. This is my mistake, Nick. We had set up Delivery Stable Blues, and we just talked our way right through it. They have never heard it, so we are now playing Delivery Stable Blues. We'll come back to Satanic Blues in a moment. The Satanic Blues The Satanic Blues The Satanic Blues The Satanic Blues The Satanic Blues And that was the Delivery Stable Blues. We've got so many interesting things that we wanted to talk to Mr. LaRocca about, but we had promised to you that we would play the Satanic Blues, but we won't be able to play too much because we have an extremely interesting story coming up. So now that we're ready, let's hear at least a portion of The Satanic Blues. The Satanic Blues We're very sorry that we couldn't finish the whole thing, but we believe that our message is just as important as the music. Now, back to Nick LaRocca. Nick, that is in the real tradition of two-beat music, as we call it, which was the original Dixieland beat. Is that correct? That's correct. And that's the only type of music you fellas knew how to play.
That's right. March syncopated.
And this was the music that you say had been born in Chicago as a sudden inspiration from the bandstand, that you had watched people dance.
That's right. But all New Orleans bars.
That's right. Now, let me ask you a question. Did you keep on writing tunes while you were in New York?
Yes, I did. I wrote many numbers.
Uh-huh.
Old Joe Blades. All my... I'd have to... If you had briefed me on that, I could give you a list of about 30 or 40 popular numbers. Rambling Blues, Toddling Blues, and Some Rainy Night.
Mm-hmm. Now, where did you get the inspiration for a lot of these things?

Well, many times I used to sit in the park at... over at Central Park and hear the band play. And like Skeleton Jangle, I heard them play a tune. I know it's a piece of opera, but what number it is, I don't know.
Oh, what is that? It went...
Well, Nick, don't you know what that is?
Yes. That's a part of the so-called trio of the Second Hungarian Rhapsody.

Yeah, well, that's where I got most all my music, by listening to a learned musician playing. And being a faker, I couldn't produce what they produce, and out would come something else. And that's where the Skeleton Jangle was born.
Well, where in the world did you get a title like the Skeleton Jangle?
Well, a fellow down in a phonograph store in Dallas, Texas, sent me up that name and asked me to name my next tune Skeleton Jangle.
Well, how do you like that?
So we had a contract with Victor to furnish 12 numbers. Well, when I went up to New York, I only had three or four put together. So I had to make eight more numbers.
I see.
Where was I going to get them from? They had to be mine. And I started working on these tunes.

So I think the best we could do right now would be to let people hear the very tune we're talking about. We do have it ready. And it's called the Skeleton Jangle, which you say you got in a Central Park band concert from the Second Hungarian Rhapsody. Is that correct? That's correct. Well, let's hear the Second Hungarian Rhapsody of the way Nick LaRocca interprets it. The Second Hungarian Rhapsody of the way Nick LaRocca interprets it. While we were playing that record, I had an opportunity to talk to our friend Nick LaRocca further, and he told me what is probably a story that has never been heard before, to the best of my knowledge. You were talking about Tiger Rag, Nick, which is also your composition. Is that right? Tiger Rag. And I find it very hard to trace this thing, but you've cleared it up. Where did Tiger Rag come from?
Well, I'll tell you where the Tiger Rag came from. If you take the inning, which is mine, and da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da, that's the inning, ain't it?
Right.
Now we'll start the first part of the tune.

same thing only a little piece of tango put into there that's London Bridge London is just falling down that little tune that I know in my babyhood days absolutely in the camouflage like a faker would do I couldn't play the tune out because people would laugh at me so we I used to go to shows and different things watch these soft shoe dances I said why why can't I make it like that so I started abbreviating the tune understand making the stop time so that's the original when it came to the chorus part is nothing other but Sousa's national anthem the court construction now that's right that in March time watch me change hold that tiger hold that tiger
so in other words from three different tunes
it's the same court construction with the weaving of my own melodies and own ideas on this court construction of John Philip Sousa's march

now in other words then tiger rag came from three different sources the first one would be uh the la paloma and London Bridge is falling down and uh what we call the chorus was uh based on the chord foundation of uh Sousa's march that's right right now let's pass along Nick uh while you fellas were over in England uh you had to change pianists as we know because Russell Robertson had to come home we all know that story and uh the rest of your boys stayed over there and you actually introduced jazz music to all of Europe through your stay in London is that correct yes our
records were sold all over the world even in Japan had our records in 1917 right and uh
you you stayed over in Europe and then you came back to the states of course and you played music uh all around for for many many years now uh when did you come back home to New Orleans
uh well you would you like me to take the part where I come back to New York and we uh where Gilda Gray had our debut at the original Vickillain Jazz Band at Follies-Berger New York City
in other words 1920 that's when you came back into New York uh but when I came back to New Orleans was in 1925 uh-huh but by that time the Dixieland Band had started to drift apart is that

correct well with white men coming in the picture and nobody and uh and petty moralists uh passing laws that they wouldn't allow us to play on Broadway we'll run off of Broadway I come here brokenhearted and
down in the dumps I can imagine now uh I was told and by and I also have read that you fellas were reorganized for a brief stay over in Dallas in 1937 is that right no we we uh was to go in the big

broadcast of 1936 but I was building a house here out on Jackson Avenue and I couldn't make it uh-huh in time I couldn't get the boys together in time oh I see then I was uh all this adverse publicity against us and it was calling this music Chicago Swing I made up my mind they were playing Dixieland idioms and I was going back in the music business to show these people that the music came from New

Orleans yeah now Nick we we're getting very close to being completely out of time now Nick we we're getting very close to being completely out of time and I wanted to deliver this message to our listening radio audience and that is that the father of Dixieland music is still with us in good health we're happy to say in the city of New Orleans but unfortunately he's house ridden because uh he cannot get around the way he should and Nick may I have your permission to give your address over this broadcast well you can do that Dave because uh I think that there are thousands of people throughout the United States would like to know and drop a card or a letter to a famous man a man who has done a great service to music and particularly to jazz music if you would write to Nick Nick LaRocca L-A-R-O-C-C-A at 22 18 Constance Street that's C-O-N-S-T-A-N-C-E 22 18 Constance Street you will make a fine gentleman happy by knowing that his message has been finally delivered after many a year now Nick we've got time for just a little more music and the one I selected was a tune that you wrote in London called Lass's Candy will you just tell us a little bit of that before we sign off well

Lass's Candy I had already I originally named it Belgian doll and the publisher didn't like the name and uh well I changed it to Lass's Candy think of the Lass's Candy we used to have in New Orleans and and molasses that they used to manufacture and put up in cans we used to eat and I said well I didn't have no other title I give it call it Lass's Candy so in other words even at the time you were in
London England your heart and your mind had never left New Orleans I never did no well I'm here
there's nothing strange that I'm here right still living in New Orleans that's typical of New Orleans

so Nick we're going to leave our radio audience now but we will never leave your music and may I tell you on behalf of not only our radio station but of all the thousands of people who listen to jazz jamboree good health good luck and may you live to see many a happy new year as long as there's good jazz and we'll leave now with your composition called Lass's Candy stuff The End The End The End The End The End The End The End

segments.title: Radio introduction of Nick LaRocca by telephone
segments.summary: Dave introduces LaRocca, 71, interviewed by phone because his legs limit him.

segments.title: Teaching himself cornet as a boy in 1898
segments.summary: LaRocca began on his musician father's cornet at about nine, against his father's wishes.

segments.title: Early string bands and free serenades in the Irish Channel
segments.summary: He played professionally around 1908 after string bands in 1902-03, with the old high-pitch cornet and unpaid party jobs.

segments.title: Record break; his own band and joining Papa Jack Laine's band
segments.summary: After a record is played, he describes the Rockus band, other New Orleans bands, and leading Laine's band 1912-16.

segments.title: Ragtime versus jazz in New Orleans before 1916
segments.summary: New Orleans bands played two-beat syncopated ragtime, not jazz, until about 1916.

segments.title: Harry James and taking a band to Chicago in 1916
segments.summary: Impresario Harry James hired him to furnish a band, taken to Chicago in March 1916.

segments.title: Nine months in Chicago and the birth of jazz
segments.summary: In Chicago the band added syncopation to a one step, the crowd demanded jazz, and the name was added to the band.

segments.title: At the Jazz Band Ball and the Delivery Stable Blues lawsuit
segments.summary: Brief talk of the tune he wrote with Shields and the injunction over Delivery Stable Blues.

segments.title: Composing as a faker from old chord constructions
segments.summary: Unable to read music, he built new tunes on chords of older pieces; the band were all fakers.

segments.chapter: Band in New York and London
segments.title: Broadway success in New York and left-handed cornet
segments.summary: The band went to Reisenweber's in New York and caused a sensation; he played cornet left-handed.

segments.chapter: Band in New York and London
segments.title: Replacements, trip to London and Satanic Blues
segments.summary: After Edwards entered the Army in 1918, Christian joined and the band took jazz to London and wrote Satanic Blues.

segments.chapter: Band in New York and London
segments.title: A cooperative band of friends, and the two-beat style
segments.summary: The band split money five ways with LaRocca as business manager; records played; March syncopated style.

segments.title: Writing more tunes and Skeleton Jangle from Hungarian Rhapsody
segments.summary: He wrote many tunes in New York, sourced Skeleton Jangle from a Central Park concert, with a Victor contract for 12 numbers.

segments.title: Origins of Tiger Rag from three sources
segments.summary: Tiger Rag combined La Paloma, London Bridge and Sousa chord structure.

segments.title: Return from Europe, decline of the band and attempted reunion
segments.summary: Records sold worldwide; return to New York in 1920, New Orleans in 1925, and a thwarted 1936 reunion.

segments.title: Sign-off, address, and the tune Lass's Candy
segments.summary: Dave gives LaRocca's address, LaRocca explains the title Lass's Candy, and the broadcast ends.
